2.question_text:
Rapid improvements in physical technologies - particularly computing and the internet - have precipitated our transition into the Information Age. These changes enhance our ability to communicate, coordinate and control, which are the underpinning drivers of both physical and social technologies. But the same innovations blur the boundaries between social and physical tools, altering what it means to be human and what it means to be a machine. Because our social orders are products of human imagination - what the historian Yuval Noah Harari calls “imagined orders” - revolutions in information technology reverberate through our institutions, identities and behaviours.

Language, writing and printing were the foundational information revolutions that created new social orders. Who could have forecast that Gutenberg’s press would catalyse the Protestant Reformation, the scientific revolution, the Enlightenment, mass culture and democratic politics? Each revolution transformed cognition, moral values and collective identity. Today, another such transformation is under way. Computers amplify our problem-solving abilities; the web extends our memory and knowledge; and connected sensors give us a kind of distributed omnipresence. These technologies alter how we think, feel and relate to others.

We are now losing our species-wide monopoly on information processing. Machine-learning algorithms make decisions once left to human judgment: diagnosing diseases, filtering job applicants, conducting stock trades and driving vehicles. They shape our opinions, our political choices, and the information we encounter. Robots assist in surgery and manufacture our automobiles. Increasingly, humans share the status of “apex information-processing species” with machines.

But technologies do not evolve to make us happier or more harmonious; they evolve because they are better at reproducing themselves. Similarly, platforms such as Facebook, Google or X propagate because they scale efficiently and because network effects create dominant winners. Their value systems arise not from ethics but from algorithms optimised for engagement, growth and profit. The result is unintended consequences: technologies that began as tools for connection have become sources of distraction, addiction and division.

Human biology exacerbates these effects. Our social cognition evolved in small tribes, where moral outrage helped maintain cohesion. But when amplified by social media, outrage becomes performative and polarising. Facial cues that normally signal empathy disappear, and our evolved desire for status fuels cascades of accusation and counter-accusation. A biological mechanism once beneficial at small scales becomes maladaptive at the scale of billions.

Meanwhile, economic and social dominance enables technologies to reproduce even faster. The platform titans of the Information Age wield unprecedented power. They shape our relationships, control flows of information, influence political processes, and mediate our economic decisions. Their reach exceeds that of the monopolies of the Industrial Age, and their algorithms determine what we see, think and value.

As the world becomes more complex, we turn to science for guidance. Yet science itself is a social technology—one that evolves unevenly. Economics illustrates this tension: its neoclassical foundations, built on assumptions of rational, self-interested utility maximisers, are poorly suited to an era defined by network effects, behavioural biases, inequality and environmental constraint. The discipline’s mechanistic models struggle to illuminate the evolutionary upheavals of the Information Age. Just as biology revolutionised medicine, complexity economics might revolutionise policymaking. But complex systems resist control. It is one thing to design a laptop; another to design the internet.

Imagined orders, information revolutions, platform dominance, machine cognition, economic certainty
Information revolutions, imagined orders, machine cognition, ethical algorithms, regulatory control
Information revolutions, imagined orders, machine cognition, platform dominance, complexity limits

6.question_text:
Life on Earth did not begin as the intricate, interconnected system we know today. When the young planet first cooled, its oceans and atmosphere obeyed the predictable laws of physics. But once life emerged in the primordial seas, that simplicity gave way to the roiling complexity of biological evolution. Primitive bacteria dominated for nearly a billion years, extracting hydrogen from hydrogen sulfide or water and using energy from the Sun or deep-sea vents. Their ability to exploit new sources of energy set off cascading feedbacks that altered the planet itself. Blue-green algae filled the atmosphere with oxygen, reshaping the chemistry of oceans and air and creating conditions for entirely new forms of life to evolve.

Oxygen, although toxic to many early organisms, also enabled life to thrive. As atmospheric oxygen accumulated, photosynthesising plants flourished, protected from harmful radiation by the ozone layer. Over immense spans of time, this oxygen-rich environment allowed a brilliant diversification: sponges, corals and jellyfish in the oceans; insects, reptiles, dinosaurs, mammals and countless other creatures on land. Each burst of life created new opportunities, and each expansion produced vulnerabilities. For every form that adapted successfully, others failed.

Throughout these eras, the Earth experienced repeated catastrophes. Around 250 million years ago, colossal volcanic eruptions spewed ash and gases that blocked sunlight and cooled the planet, destroying most life forms, including trilobites and many marine species. Sixty-six million years ago, a comet collided with the Earth, again darkening the skies and wiping out nearly all dinosaurs. Yet life persisted because diversity—across species, within species, and even within individuals—served as nature’s insurance against collapse. Some organisms could adjust, some could migrate and some could simply endure until conditions stabilised.

Nature’s long experience offers a powerful lesson: diversity is essential for resilience in complex systems. Today, humanity faces analogous threats in the form of climate change, pandemics and disruptions to global food and resource networks. Yet our food supply depends increasingly on a narrow range of genetically similar crop species, making us more vulnerable to climatic shocks. Nature’s example suggests the wisdom of maintaining variety—not just in plants and animals but also in cultures, knowledge systems and ways of thinking. Diversity in finance provides stability through varied portfolios, while design diversity in engineering offers built-in redundancy. Seed banks, conservation practices and the preservation of indigenous knowledge are all modern expressions of nature’s strategy.

The importance of diversity becomes clearer when seen against the backdrop of nature’s catastrophic history. Without a varied ecological community, life might not have recovered after massive volcanic winters or comet impacts. Each survivor lineage carried forward the potential for future complexity. Just as ecosystems benefit from diverse species and functions, human societies benefit from multiple perspectives, distributed knowledge, and networks that avoid dangerous single points of failure.

The deep past demonstrates that complexity brings both risk and opportunity. Catastrophes will continue to emerge from unpredictable directions, but systems with multiple pathways for survival—whether ecological or human—are far better positioned to adapt. Nature’s experience, accumulated over billions of years, suggests that resilience does not come from eliminating uncertainty but from cultivating variety and flexibility within it. In an increasingly interconnected world, this may be the most important lesson of all.

Which of the following best describes the central concern of the passage?
options: The role of complexity in enabling resilience in both natural and human systems.
The evolutionary process as a constant interplay between new opportunities and vulnerabilities.
The importance of diversity in enabling resilience in natural and human systems.
The capacity of complex systems to withstand repeated disruptions.

The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
A new theoretical proposal suggests that gravity is not a fundamental force of nature but an emergent phenomenon arising from quantum electromagnetic interactions. Developed by Ruth Kastner and Andreas Schlatter, the theory argues that spacetime itself is not basic, but emerges from exchanges of photons between charged particles such as atoms and molecules. These “transactions” create interconnected spacetime events that collectively produce what we perceive as space, time, and gravity. Instead of treating gravity as a distinct force, the researchers explain gravitational attraction through thermodynamics and entropy. As mass increases, so does the number of possible quantum interactions, naturally generating an attractive effect. This approach can reproduce key predictions of general relativity without requiring gravity to be fundamental. The model also offers alternative explanations for dark matter and dark energy, suggesting they emerge from ordinary matter’s behavior rather than unknown substances. While still speculative, the theory provides a potential new path toward unifying quantum mechanics and gravity.
options: A new theoretical proposal argues that gravity and spacetime are emergent outcomes of quantum electromagnetic interactions, rather than fundamental features of nature.
A new theoretical proposal replaces gravity with electromagnetic forces, claiming that photon exchanges directly generate gravitational pull between massive objects.
The researchers of a new theoretical model propose that entropy-driven quantum interactions can account for gravity and cosmological phenomena without invoking dark matter.
A new theoretical model challenges general relativity by rejecting its predictions and offering a competing framework rooted entirely in quantum mechanics.

13.question_text:
Cats seem to be succeeding at world domination; they live on every continent except Antarctica. While researchers know that modern house cats descended from the African wildcat, exactly how, when and where domestic cats became benevolent dictators of human households remains debated. Now, two genetic analyses suggest that domestic cats reached Europe and China far later than once thought.

Past research held that cats began living with humans east of the Mediterranean almost 10,000 years ago, leading to the idea that domestic kitties traveled to Europe about 6,500 years ago with Neolithic farmers. In the new work, scientists set out to determine which ancient cat bones—long assumed to be domestic—actually carried genomes similar to those of modern cats. But many remains turned out to be wildcats, which upends the earlier narrative and reveals a far more tangled history between humans and felines. Unlike domestic dogs, whose physical changes make them easily distinguishable from wolves, cats have stayed so similar to their wild relatives that telling them apart in ancient remains is notoriously difficult.

In the study tracing ancestry in Europe, researchers analyzed 225 cat specimens from nearly 100 archaeological sites across Europe and Anatolia. These yielded 87 genomes spanning 11,000 years. The analysis showed that cats in Europe before 200 B.C.E. were wildcats, and that domestic cats didn’t arrive there until roughly 2,000 years ago. Surprisingly, they came not from east of the Mediterranean but from North Africa. The study also found two distinct cat populations in Europe originating in North Africa. In the early modern world, few institutions embodied the fusion of commerce, state power and global ambition as dramatically as the Dutch East India Company. Emerging in a period when European states sought direct access to Asian spices, the Dutch enterprise quickly eclipsed rivals in scale and organization. Investors had grasped that a single successful voyage could yield extraordinary returns, and early expeditions confirmed these expectations. Dutch fleets secured cargoes of pepper and other valuable goods, generating profits that galvanized further participation. By the end of the sixteenth century, multiple Dutch companies were sending dozens of ships to the East, welcomed by local communities who viewed them as effective counterweights to Portuguese dominance.

Paradoxically, the very success of these ventures threatened their future. As Dutch companies multiplied and competed, they drove down spice prices in Europe and raised purchasing costs in Asia. Alarmed investors recognized that internal competition weakened their position against Iberian rivals. Their remedy was radical: they would consolidate into a single entity with exclusive rights to Asian trade. After prolonged debate among the provinces, the States General authorized a unified company with a twenty-one-year monopoly. Thus, in 1602, the Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie, or VOC, was born.

The company’s governance reflected both Dutch republican concerns and commercial priorities. A “Council of Seventeen” balanced regional interests, preventing Amsterdam—the nation’s most powerful commercial center—from dominating decision-making. Shares were open in principle to all citizens, but in practice the company soon came under the control of a small cadre of wealthy merchants whose capital was committed for long periods rather than single voyages. This structure produced what many consider the world’s first joint-stock corporation: a permanent, investor-funded enterprise whose shares were traded on an emerging stock exchange and whose scale dwarfed its contemporaries.

Yet the VOC was far more than a commercial concern. Unusually for a private company, it was endowed with quasi-sovereign powers. It could negotiate treaties, wage war, build fortifications, administer justice, mint currency and establish colonies—all nominally in the name of the Dutch state, yet largely free of direct governmental oversight. In effect, it operated as a state within a state, projecting Dutch influence across thousands of miles with a mixture of diplomacy, intimidation and force.

This mixture proved decisive. VOC fleets were dispatched not only to trade but to seize strategic positions and attack Portuguese strongholds. Their ships were as heavily laden with armaments as with commodities, and their military campaigns were often more successful than those of many European nations. The capture of the Portuguese fort at Ambon marked the beginning of a rapid territorial expansion. Within a few years, the VOC controlled a dense network of ports, factories and garrisons from the Arabian coast to Japan.

Although celebrated for its commercial achievements, the company’s rise was inseparable from violence. As one historian observed, its military capacity initially outweighed its trading function; it was “less a capitalist firm than a syndicate for piracy,” financed by private investors but wielding power on behalf of a state. Through this combination of profit seeking and armed coercion, the VOC became one of the most formidable institutions of its age.

According to the passage, the initial success of Dutch trading voyages eventually became a problem chiefly because:
options: Individual Dutch fleets began attacking one another’s cargo ships to secure a larger share of the Asian spice trade.
Rising competition among Dutch companies pushed prices up in Europe while lowering what traders paid for goods in Asia.
Multiplying, competing Dutch companies pushed European prices down and Asian purchase costs up, eroding profits just when unity against the Portuguese mattered most.
The Portuguese responded to Dutch gains by lowering their own prices, undercutting Dutch companies across European markets.
